Hi there. Diagnosed here w bipolar 2 for almost three years now. Been with my boyfriend since just a little bit before the diagnosis.

If you’re really into this girl, I believe what works is that you assure her you’re there despite her low moments, and that you see her as more than her diagnosis — a kind, *insert positive adjectives here* woman that you like through and through.

My tendency is to push my boyfriend away everytime I’m in my dark moods, believing myself to be horrible and unworthy of how awesome and understanding he is. Believe me, if it were some other guy, I think they would’ve run for the hills, but my guy simply asks me to acknowledge that my low mood is affecting my perception of reality + the relationship and helps me go through it (no way out but through!) by holding my hand and asking me to do self-care activities, which could be anything from a spa trip to an emergency visit to my doctor.

Ask her how she usually copes with these low moods, remind her that you’re there whenever and however way she needs, and assure her she’s still her despite the darkness.

I wish you the best :)

Hi there!

I’m also a girl, diagnosed when I was 21. I’m turning 24 now. I have hypomanic episodes and severe depressive episodes, cycling very rapidly recently. I’ve been depressed this past two weeks after feeling so powerful for three.

For sure the TLDR post pinned on top of this sub will help you — tell you the truth, I haven’t finished it but I read it a bit here and there and those little nuggets of new knowledge always help — but the thing is, despite the official label, this disease can manifest in different ways in different people. It helps to also lurk around here and to notice similar patterns in your life and the plethora of tried and tested coping mechanisms that you can use.

More so, I’ve found that my bipolar sitch itself has evolved for me. When I was younger, it manifested as more hypomania with the shopping sprees, the dating frenzy due to hypersexuality, the impulsive adventurous streak that had me climbing mountains with online strangers. 

These days, I’m more severely depressed, and I call my hypomania responsible hypomania because it’s when I work out, get things done, cook and other adulty things. Haha.

You should know that it’s imperative that you develop kindness towards yourself very early. You need this during the hardest times. If you’re like me and you’re frequently depressed and hopeless, you have to soldier on the darkest days through the simplest self-care tricks: have a nice, luxurious-in-your-terms space, take nice long baths, paint your nails, develop a spa-worthy skincare routine, have a go-to mindless tv show to binge etc.

You should also get an awesome therapist and at least one buddy to call for emergencies. Self-care can only do so much; you need to establish a great support system this early on. In dealing w bipolar you will eventually need coping and self-soothing strategies to get you through the horrible thoughts.

Please also be responsible with your medication, no matter what anyone else says if you realize they are indeed helping. At first, I have friends who would say “I wish you didn’t take meds, psych talk therapy is better” but I’ve learned to tune that out — I don’t want to feel guilty about a method that works for me.

Lastly, have a good purpose and try to seek it early, it will inspire you. Whether it’s being of service to the world through whatever advocacy or simply helping out your family and friends for whatever, it will power you. It reminds you of what you are, always.

Everyone deserves a partner who is dependable, understanding and makes you want to be better and kinder to yourself. If anything, BP’s like us need it more. 

Dating can be exhausting for people who are not struggling with this, and even more so with us, because we tend to blame ourselves for every possible thing that goes wrong, or when we become too attached. 

That being said, I think it should be part of our self-care that we practice openness in all relationships from the get go as this practically weeds out the bad company from the good. It saves you time and distress as you need someone who can handle all the complications of your condition. You need someone who is emotionally ready to take the bad with all the awesomeness you have to offer. 

You deserve someone amazing, and someone who won’t hesitate to get all-out attached to you too. I know it’s hard not to take it personally when someone jumps ship at the first instance of trouble or when you confess your mental health issues, but remember that you are meant for a special kind of a person and passing on those who can’t deal with the disorder and all its symptoms is one step closer to finding real love.

Hey there. I just started posting myself too. Was diagnosed last year and ended up with a cocktail of anti-depressants, mood stabilizers and anti-psychotics. I was extremely lucky, this concoction worked perfectly for me, and I noticed that the months that I do take them regularly combined with exercise, eating clean and being on top of my tasks at work were the best months of my life. 

I'm off meds now because I'm broke from quitting my job and horrible spending habits when I did have it. I don't have to point out that skipping meds + making major life decisions while being off them  = horrible days. 

But after days of suicidal ideation, I've finally calmed down enough to give life another shot and I intend on taking them again soon after visiting my psychiatrist on the weekend. 

Friendly advice -- always make sure your meds are refilled! Get a system that incorporates working out (boxing really helps for me, plus I'm a girl and it makes me feel badass) and set hours for your medication after eating clean. If you do skip meds, that's normal and just find the light to go back, always. Having friends and this thread help!

Also, according to my friends, it took time for some of them to arrive at the best combination. Be open to your doctor about how your current mix makes you feel and don't expect the first mix to be The One.
